items.stem: Which groups react to form a peptide bond?
items.answer: the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of another
items.markingKey: the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of another. Condensation releases water.

items.stem: Explain why the diversity of proteins is so great.
items.answer: There are 20 amino acids and they can be joined in any sequence; chains vary in length from a few to thousands; 20ⁿ possible sequences; each sequence folds into a specific shape giving a specific function.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There are 20 amino acids and they can be joined in any sequence; chains vary in length from a few to thousands; 20ⁿ possible sequences; each sequence folds into a specific shape giving a specific function. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which property of an amino acid is determined by its R group?
options: whether it is polar, non-polar, acidic or basic
the number of carbon atoms in its backbone
whether it can form a peptide bond
items.answer: whether it is polar, non-polar, acidic or basic
items.markingKey: B. All amino acids share the backbone; R groups differ.

items.stem: A protein has two polypeptide chains of 141 and 146 amino acids. How many peptide bonds does it contain?
A bacterial enzyme consists of 1 polypeptide chain containing 182 amino acids. Calculate the number of peptide bonds and the number of water molecules released during its synthesis.
items.answer: 181 peptide bonds; 181 water molecules
items.markingKey: Each chain of n amino acids has n − 1 bonds (M1); total 182 − 1 = 181 bonds, one water per bond (A1).

items.stem: Describe the structure of amino acids and explain how they are joined to form a huge variety of polypeptides.
items.answer: General structure: central C, NH₂, COOH, H, R; R groups vary (20 types, polar/non-polar/charged); peptide bond by condensation on ribosomes; water released; N- and C-terminus; any sequence; 20ⁿ; genetic code determines sequence; essential vs non-essential.
items.markingKey: General structure: central C, NH₂, COOH, H, R; R groups vary (20 types, polar/non-polar/charged); peptide bond by condensation on ribosomes; water released; N- and C-terminus; any sequence; 20ⁿ; genetic code determines sequence; essential vs non-essential.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "R group"?
options: A covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine R groups, which stabilises tertiary or quaternary structure
A protein with a compact, rounded, usually water-soluble shape, often with a metabolic role, such as insulin or enzymes
The variable side chain of an amino acid, which determines its properties (e.g. polar, non-polar, charged)
The monomer of proteins, with a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R group
items.answer: The variable side chain of an amino acid, which determines its properties (e.g. polar, non-polar, charged)
items.markingKey: C. "R group" is the variable side chain of an amino acid, which determines its properties (e.g. polar, non-polar, charged).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "All amino acids have the same R group." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The R group is the variable part; 20 different R groups give the different amino acids.
items.markingKey: The R group is the variable part; 20 different R groups give the different amino acids. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between non-essential amino acids and essential amino acids.
items.answer: Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from the diet; non-essential amino acids can be synthesised from other compounds.
items.markingKey: Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from the diet; non-essential amino acids can be synthesised from other compounds. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the dietary combination of rice and lentils in South Asian cooking (dal-bhat) and explain what it reveals about essential amino acids.
items.answer: Rice is low in lysine and lentils are low in methionine; together they supply all essential amino acids. Combining plant proteins with different deficiencies supplies all the amino acids the body cannot make.
items.markingKey: Context (Rice is low in lysine and lentils are low in methionine; together they supply all essential amino acids.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Combining plant proteins with different deficiencies supplies all the amino acids the body cannot make. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to essential amino acids.

items.stem:
Samples of lactate dehydrogenase from rabbit muscle (enzyme X) and a homologous enzyme from the archaeon Pyrococcus furiosus (enzyme Y) were held at different temperatures for 10 minutes, cooled to 25 °C and their remaining activity measured as a percentage of the untreated activity.

Temperature / °C | Enzyme X activity remaining / % | Enzyme Y activity remaining / %
30 | 100 | 100
40 | 99 | 100
50 | 91 | 100
60 | 36 | 100
70 | 3 | 99
80 | 0 | 80
90 | 0 | 19

(a) State the activity of enzyme X remaining after treatment at 60 °C. [1]
(b) Estimate the temperature at which each enzyme has lost half of its activity. [2]
(c) Compare the effect of temperature on enzymes X and Y. [2]
items.answer: (a) 36 % (b) X ≈ 57 °C; Y ≈ 85 °C (c) Both retain full activity at low temperatures and lose activity as temperature rises; Y tolerates much higher temperatures before losing activity.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 36 % (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation (M1); X 57 °C and Y 85 °C, accept ±2 °C (A1). (c) [2] Similarity (A1); difference with data (A1).

items.stem: "The 20 amino acids are enough to produce all the protein diversity found in living things." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Twenty amino acids give more than enough diversity in principle; real diversity is extended by modifications and a few rare amino acids, but limited by folding constraints.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: 20ⁿ possible sequences is astronomically large even for short chains; post-translational modifications add further diversity. Arguments against: some organisms use additional amino acids such as selenocysteine and pyrrolysine; only a tiny fraction of possible sequences fold into stable, functional proteins. Supported judgement: Twenty amino acids give more than enough diversity in principle; real diversity is extended by modifications and a few rare amino acids, but limited by folding constraints. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which level of structure is directly determined by the gene sequence?
items.answer: primary structure
items.markingKey: primary structure. Higher levels follow from the primary sequence.

items.stem: "Secondary structure is stabilised by bonds between R groups." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Secondary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone; R-group interactions stabilise tertiary structure.
items.markingKey: Secondary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone; R-group interactions stabilise tertiary structure. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between tertiary structure and quaternary structure.
items.answer: Tertiary structure is the 3D folding of a single polypeptide; quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptides (and prosthetic groups) in a protein.
items.markingKey: Tertiary structure is the 3D folding of a single polypeptide; quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptides (and prosthetic groups) in a protein. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which sickle-cell haemoglobin (HbS) shows the link between primary structure and protein shape.
items.answer: A single substitution of valine for glutamic acid on the β chain causes haemoglobin to polymerise at low oxygen, distorting red cells into sickle shapes. One change in sequence alters R-group interactions, so the shape and behaviour of the whole protein change.
items.markingKey: Context (A single substitution of valine for glutamic acid on the β chain causes haemoglobin to polymerise at low oxygen, distorting red cells into sickle shapes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: One change in sequence alters R-group interactions, so the shape and behaviour of the whole protein change. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the link between primary structure and protein shape.

items.stem: A protein retains its function after treatment with a reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds, but loses it after heating. What does this suggest?
options: Its shape depends mainly on non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
Its shape depends only on disulfide bonds.
items.answer: Its shape depends mainly on non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
items.markingKey: C. Heat disrupts weak interactions.

items.stem:
Samples of a protease from cod (a cold-water fish) (enzyme X) and the same enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium (enzyme Y) were held at different temperatures for 10 minutes, cooled to 25 °C and their remaining activity measured as a percentage of the untreated activity.

Temperature / °C | Enzyme X activity remaining / % | Enzyme Y activity remaining / %
30 | 100 | 100
40 | 97 | 100
50 | 67 | 100
60 | 10 | 100
70 | 1 | 98
80 | 0 | 71
90 | 0 | 12

(a) State the activity of enzyme X remaining after treatment at 60 °C. [1]
(b) Estimate the temperature at which each enzyme has lost half of its activity. [2]
(c) Compare the effect of temperature on enzymes X and Y. [2]
(d) Explain why activity was measured at 25 °C after cooling, rather than at the treatment temperature. [1]
items.answer: (a) 10 % (b) X ≈ 53 °C; Y ≈ 84 °C (c) Both retain full activity at low temperatures and lose activity as temperature rises; Y tolerates much higher temperatures before losing activity. (d) It measures only the permanent (irreversible) loss of activity due to denaturation, not the temporary effect of temperature on reaction rate.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 10 % (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation (M1); X 53 °C and Y 84 °C, accept ±2 °C (A1). (c) [2] Similarity (A1); difference with data (A1). (d) [1] Separates denaturation from effect on rate (R1).

items.stem: Describe the four levels of protein structure and explain how each is stabilised.
items.answer: Primary: sequence, peptide bonds, gene-determined. Secondary: α-helix, β-sheet, H bonds in backbone. Tertiary: 3D fold, R-group interactions – hydrophobic, H bonds, ionic, disulfide. Quaternary: multiple subunits, e.g. haemoglobin (4 subunits + haem), collagen (3 chains); conjugated vs non-conjugated. Shape determines function.
items.markingKey: Primary: sequence, peptide bonds, gene-determined. Secondary: α-helix, β-sheet, H bonds in backbone. Tertiary: 3D fold, R-group interactions – hydrophobic, H bonds, ionic, disulfide. Quaternary: multiple subunits, e.g. haemoglobin (4 subunits + haem), collagen (3 chains); conjugated vs non-conjugated. Shape determines function.

items.stem: "The primary structure of a protein completely determines its final shape." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Primary structure contains the information for folding, but the cellular environment, chaperones and modifications influence the final, functional shape.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Anfinsen showed denatured ribonuclease refolds spontaneously into its active shape; AI structure prediction from sequence is highly accurate. Arguments against: many proteins need chaperones to fold correctly in cells; post-translational modifications and prosthetic groups also affect structure; prions can adopt alternative shapes. Supported judgement: Primary structure contains the information for folding, but the cellular environment, chaperones and modifications influence the final, functional shape. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "secondary structure".
items.answer: Regular folding of the polypeptide backbone into α-helices or β-pleated sheets, stabilised by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: regular folding of the polypeptide backbone into α-helices or β-pleated sheets, stabilised by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how the primary structure of a protein determines its three-dimensional shape.
items.answer: The sequence of amino acids determines where hydrogen bonds form in the backbone (α-helices, β-sheets) and where R groups interact (hydrophobic clustering, ionic, hydrogen and disulfide bonds), so the chain folds into one specific stable conformation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The sequence of amino acids determines where hydrogen bonds form in the backbone (α-helices, β-sheets) and where R groups interact (hydrophobic clustering, ionic, hydrogen and disulfide bonds), so the chain folds into one specific stable conformation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why can a single amino acid substitution change the function of a protein?
options: It may alter R-group interactions, changing the tertiary structure and shape.
It removes the quaternary structure in all proteins.
It always breaks all peptide bonds.
items.answer: It may alter R-group interactions, changing the tertiary structure and shape.
items.markingKey: A. E.g. sickle-cell haemoglobin.

items.stem: In sickle-cell haemoglobin, a glutamic acid (charged, polar) at position 6 of the β chain is replaced by valine (non-polar). What is the most likely effect?
options: Hydrophobic patches on the surface cause haemoglobin molecules to stick together into fibres at low oxygen.
The protein can no longer form peptide bonds.
The protein becomes a fibrous structural protein.
items.answer: Hydrophobic patches on the surface cause haemoglobin molecules to stick together into fibres at low oxygen.
items.markingKey: A. Altered surface properties cause polymerisation.

items.stem: Briefly describe AlphaFold’s prediction of protein structures from sequences (2020–2022) and explain what it reveals about how primary structure determines tertiary structure.
items.answer: An AI system predicted 3D structures of over 200 million proteins from their amino acid sequences with high accuracy. Accurate prediction from sequence alone confirms that the amino acid sequence encodes the folded shape.
items.markingKey: Context (An AI system predicted 3D structures of over 200 million proteins from their amino acid sequences with high accuracy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Accurate prediction from sequence alone confirms that the amino acid sequence encodes the folded shape. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how primary structure determines tertiary structure.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "All proteins have quaternary structure." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Only proteins made of more than one polypeptide (e.g. haemoglobin, collagen) have quaternary structure; many enzymes are single polypeptides.
items.markingKey: Only proteins made of more than one polypeptide (e.g. haemoglobin, collagen) have quaternary structure; many enzymes are single polypeptides. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: How does extreme pH cause denaturation?
items.answer: by changing the charges on R groups, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds
items.markingKey: by changing the charges on R groups, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds. H⁺ or OH⁻ alter ionisation of R groups.

items.stem: Explain how changes in pH affect protein structure.
items.answer: H⁺ and OH⁻ ions change the ionisation of acidic and basic R groups; this alters charges, breaking ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds between R groups; the tertiary structure changes and the protein may denature.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: H⁺ and OH⁻ ions change the ionisation of acidic and basic R groups; this alters charges, breaking ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds between R groups; the tertiary structure changes and the protein may denature. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between reversible denaturation and irreversible denaturation.
items.answer: In reversible denaturation the protein refolds to its active shape when conditions return to normal (e.g. mild pH change); in irreversible denaturation the unfolded chains aggregate or form new bonds so the original shape cannot be regained (e.g. cooked egg).
items.markingKey: In reversible denaturation the protein refolds to its active shape when conditions return to normal (e.g. mild pH change); in irreversible denaturation the unfolded chains aggregate or form new bonds so the original shape cannot be regained (e.g. cooked egg). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Enzymes are killed by high temperatures." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Enzymes are molecules, not living organisms; they are denatured, not killed.
items.markingKey: Enzymes are molecules, not living organisms; they are denatured, not killed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Egg white turns from clear to opaque white when cooked. Which explanation is correct?
options: Albumin proteins denature and aggregate, scattering light.
Albumin is hydrolysed into amino acids.
items.answer: Albumin proteins denature and aggregate, scattering light.
items.markingKey: B. Unfolded proteins clump together.

items.stem: Explain how temperature and pH affect protein structure and function, with reference to named examples.
items.answer: Weak bonds maintain shape; heat increases vibration, breaks H bonds/hydrophobic interactions; unfolds; loss of function; often irreversible (egg albumin); pH alters R-group ionisation, breaks ionic/H bonds; optimum pH (pepsin 2, trypsin 8); thermophile proteins (Taq) more stable; homeostasis maintains conditions.
items.markingKey: Weak bonds maintain shape; heat increases vibration, breaks H bonds/hydrophobic interactions; unfolds; loss of function; often irreversible (egg albumin); pH alters R-group ionisation, breaks ionic/H bonds; optimum pH (pepsin 2, trypsin 8); thermophile proteins (Taq) more stable; homeostasis maintains conditions.

items.stem: Define the term "denaturation".
items.answer: A change in the three-dimensional structure of a protein, caused by breaking of the bonds that maintain it, so that it loses its biological activity

items.stem: Why do proteins from thermophilic archaea not denature at 80 °C?
options: They are made of different amino acids not found in other organisms.
They have more ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions stabilising their structure.
items.answer: They have more ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions stabilising their structure.
items.markingKey: D. Extra stabilising interactions resist heat.

items.stem: Outline one way in which pepsin in the human stomach shows the effect of pH on protein structure.
items.answer: Pepsin works best at pH about 2 and becomes inactive in the near-neutral small intestine. Its R-group charges are suited to strong acid; at neutral pH the changed ionisation alters its shape.
items.markingKey: Context (Pepsin works best at pH about 2 and becomes inactive in the near-neutral small intestine.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Its R-group charges are suited to strong acid; at neutral pH the changed ionisation alters its shape. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of pH on protein structure.

items.stem: "Denaturation is always harmful to organisms." Discuss.
items.answer: Denaturation of an organism’s own proteins is harmful, but denaturation of food and pathogen proteins can be beneficial; the effect depends on whose proteins are denatured.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: loss of enzyme function at high fever temperatures can be fatal; heat stroke denatures cellular proteins. Arguments against: cooking denatures food proteins, making them easier to digest; denaturation of pathogen proteins by stomach acid or fever helps defence. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A small globular hormone of two polypeptide chains linked by disulfide bonds, which binds to receptors to lower blood glucose"?
items.answer: insulin

items.stem: Why are globular proteins usually soluble in water?
options: Hydrophilic R groups are on the outside and hydrophobic ones are buried inside.
items.answer: Hydrophilic R groups are on the outside and hydrophobic ones are buried inside.

items.stem: Distinguish between fibrous proteins and globular proteins.
items.answer: Fibrous proteins are long, narrow, insoluble, with repetitive sequences and structural roles (collagen, keratin); globular proteins are compact, rounded, usually soluble, with varied sequences and metabolic roles (enzymes, insulin, haemoglobin).
items.markingKey: Fibrous proteins are long, narrow, insoluble, with repetitive sequences and structural roles (collagen, keratin); globular proteins are compact, rounded, usually soluble, with varied sequences and metabolic roles (enzymes, insulin, haemoglobin). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "All proteins are enzymes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Proteins have many roles: structural (collagen), hormones (insulin), transport (haemoglobin), defence (antibodies), movement (actin/myosin) as well as enzymes.
items.markingKey: Proteins have many roles: structural (collagen), hormones (insulin), transport (haemoglobin), defence (antibodies), movement (actin/myosin) as well as enzymes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe scurvy in sailors on long voyages in the 18th century and explain what it reveals about the structure and function of collagen.
items.answer: Lack of vitamin C caused bleeding gums, reopening of old wounds and weakened tissues. Vitamin C is needed to stabilise collagen; without it, collagen fibres are weak, showing the importance of structure for function.
items.markingKey: Context (Lack of vitamin C caused bleeding gums, reopening of old wounds and weakened tissues.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Classifying proteins as fibrous or globular is a useful simplification."
items.answer: It is a useful first framework but must be supplemented by more detailed structural classification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it links shape to function in a memorable way; it predicts solubility and role. Arguments against: some proteins, such as myosin, have both fibrous and globular regions; membrane proteins fit neither category well. Supported judgement: It is a useful first framework but must be supplemented by more detailed structural classification.

A protein with a compact, rounded, usually water-soluble shape, often with a metabolic role, such as insulin or enzymes
The association of two or more polypeptide subunits (and sometimes prosthetic groups) into a functional protein
The variable side chain of an amino acid, which determines its properties (e.g. polar, non-polar, charged)
items.answer: A protein with a compact, rounded, usually water-soluble shape, often with a metabolic role, such as insulin or enzymes
items.markingKey: B. "globular protein" is a protein with a compact, rounded, usually water-soluble shape, often with a metabolic role, such as insulin or enzymes.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of collagen is related to its function.
items.answer: Three polypeptide chains wound in a tight triple helix; glycine every third position allows close packing; hydrogen bonds between chains; molecules cross-linked into fibrils and fibres; so collagen is strong, inelastic and insoluble, ideal for tendons, skin and bone.

items.stem: Vitamin C is needed to modify proline in collagen. Sailors with scurvy had bleeding gums and poor wound healing. What is the best explanation?

items.answer: On the ribosome, the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of the next in a condensation reaction; a peptide bond (–CO–NH–) forms and water is released; repetition produces a chain with an N-terminus and C-terminus.

items.answer: In reversible denaturation the protein refolds to its active shape when conditions return to normal (e.g. mild pH change); in irreversible denaturation the unfolded chains aggregate or form new bonds so the original shape cannot be regained (e.g. cooked egg).
items.markingKey: In reversible denaturation the protein refolds to its active shape when conditions return to normal (e.g. mild pH change); in irreversible denaturation the unfolded chains aggregate or form new bonds so the original shape cannot be regained (e.g. cooked egg). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Fibrous proteins dissolve easily in blood plasma." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Fibrous proteins are generally insoluble; globular proteins tend to be soluble.
items.markingKey: Fibrous proteins are generally insoluble; globular proteins tend to be soluble. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which interactions stabilise tertiary structure?
options: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions between R groups
items.answer: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions between R groups
items.markingKey: B. Several types of R-group interaction.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Peptide bonds are formed by hydrolysis." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Peptide bonds are formed by condensation (water released); hydrolysis breaks them.
items.markingKey: Peptide bonds are formed by condensation (water released); hydrolysis breaks them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using pepsin in the human stomach as an example, explain the effect of pH on protein structure.
items.answer: Pepsin works best at pH about 2 and becomes inactive in the near-neutral small intestine. Its R-group charges are suited to strong acid; at neutral pH the changed ionisation alters its shape.
items.markingKey: Context (Pepsin works best at pH about 2 and becomes inactive in the near-neutral small intestine.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Its R-group charges are suited to strong acid; at neutral pH the changed ionisation alters its shape. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of pH on protein structure.

items.stem: Outline one way in which scurvy in sailors on long voyages in the 18th century shows the structure and function of collagen.
items.answer: Lack of vitamin C caused bleeding gums, reopening of old wounds and weakened tissues. Vitamin C is needed to stabilise collagen; without it, collagen fibres are weak, showing the importance of structure for function.
items.markingKey: Context (Lack of vitamin C caused bleeding gums, reopening of old wounds and weakened tissues.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Vitamin C is needed to stabilise collagen; without it, collagen fibres are weak, showing the importance of structure for function. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the structure and function of collagen.

items.stem: Outline one way in which AlphaFold’s prediction of protein structures from sequences (2020–2022) shows how primary structure determines tertiary structure.
items.answer: An AI system predicted 3D structures of over 200 million proteins from their amino acid sequences with high accuracy. Accurate prediction from sequence alone confirms that the amino acid sequence encodes the folded shape.
items.markingKey: Context (An AI system predicted 3D structures of over 200 million proteins from their amino acid sequences with high accuracy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Accurate prediction from sequence alone confirms that the amino acid sequence encodes the folded shape. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how primary structure determines tertiary structure.

items.stem: How many different tripeptides could be made from the 20 amino acids?
Aiko writes: "Enzymes are killed by high temperatures." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Enzymes are molecules, not living organisms; they are denatured, not killed.
items.markingKey: Enzymes are molecules, not living organisms; they are denatured, not killed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Samples of a protease from the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis (enzyme X) and a protease from Thermus aquaticus (enzyme Y) were held at different temperatures for 10 minutes, cooled to 25 °C and their remaining activity measured as a percentage of the untreated activity.

Temperature / °C | Enzyme X activity remaining / % | Enzyme Y activity remaining / %
30 | 100 | 100
40 | 97 | 100
50 | 64 | 100
60 | 9 | 100
70 | 1 | 95
80 | 0 | 54
90 | 0 | 6

(a) State the activity of enzyme X remaining after treatment at 60 °C. [1]
(b) Estimate the temperature at which each enzyme has lost half of its activity. [2]
(c) Compare the effect of temperature on enzymes X and Y. [2]
items.answer: (a) 9 % (b) X ≈ 53 °C; Y ≈ 81 °C (c) Both retain full activity at low temperatures and lose activity as temperature rises; Y tolerates much higher temperatures before losing activity.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 9 % (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation (M1); X 53 °C and Y 81 °C, accept ±2 °C (A1). (c) [2] Similarity (A1); difference with data (A1).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The primary structure of a protein completely determines its final shape."
items.answer: Primary structure contains the information for folding, but the cellular environment, chaperones and modifications influence the final, functional shape.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Anfinsen showed denatured ribonuclease refolds spontaneously into its active shape; AI structure prediction from sequence is highly accurate. Arguments against: many proteins need chaperones to fold correctly in cells; post-translational modifications and prosthetic groups also affect structure; prions can adopt alternative shapes. Supported judgement: Primary structure contains the information for folding, but the cellular environment, chaperones and modifications influence the final, functional shape.

items.stem: "The 20 amino acids are enough to produce all the protein diversity found in living things." Discuss.
items.answer: Twenty amino acids give more than enough diversity in principle; real diversity is extended by modifications and a few rare amino acids, but limited by folding constraints.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: 20ⁿ possible sequences is astronomically large even for short chains; post-translational modifications add further diversity. Arguments against: some organisms use additional amino acids such as selenocysteine and pyrrolysine; only a tiny fraction of possible sequences fold into stable, functional proteins. Supported judgement: Twenty amino acids give more than enough diversity in principle; real diversity is extended by modifications and a few rare amino acids, but limited by folding constraints. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Denaturation is always harmful to organisms." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Denaturation of an organism’s own proteins is harmful, but denaturation of food and pathogen proteins can be beneficial; the effect depends on whose proteins are denatured.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: loss of enzyme function at high fever temperatures can be fatal; heat stroke denatures cellular proteins. Arguments against: cooking denatures food proteins, making them easier to digest; denaturation of pathogen proteins by stomach acid or fever helps defence. Supported judgement: Denaturation of an organism’s own proteins is harmful, but denaturation of food and pathogen proteins can be beneficial; the effect depends on whose proteins are denatured. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Classifying proteins as fibrous or globular is a useful simplification." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is a useful first framework but must be supplemented by more detailed structural classification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it links shape to function in a memorable way; it predicts solubility and role. Arguments against: some proteins, such as myosin, have both fibrous and globular regions; membrane proteins fit neither category well. Supported judgement: It is a useful first framework but must be supplemented by more detailed structural classification. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "conjugated protein"?
options: A protein that contains a non-polypeptide component (prosthetic group), such as the haem in haemoglobin
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, determined by the base sequence of a gene
The variable side chain of an amino acid, which determines its properties (e.g. polar, non-polar, charged)
The monomer of proteins, with a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R group
items.answer: A protein that contains a non-polypeptide component (prosthetic group), such as the haem in haemoglobin
items.markingKey: A. "conjugated protein" is a protein that contains a non-polypeptide component (prosthetic group), such as the haem in haemoglobin.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "essential amino acid".
items.answer: An amino acid that cannot be synthesised by the body and must be obtained from the diet
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an amino acid that cannot be synthesised by the body and must be obtained from the diet. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The pH at which a protein (such as an enzyme) is most stable and active"?
items.answer: optimum pH
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of optimum pH.

items.stem: Why must insulin have a precise globular shape?
options: It must bind specifically to insulin receptors on target cells.
items.answer: It must bind specifically to insulin receptors on target cells.
items.markingKey: D. Shape-dependent binding.

items.stem: Explain how the quaternary structure of haemoglobin relates to its function.
items.answer: Four polypeptide subunits (two α, two β) each hold a haem group with iron that binds O₂; interactions between subunits allow cooperative binding, so oxygen is loaded efficiently in the lungs and unloaded in tissues.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Four polypeptide subunits (two α, two β) each hold a haem group with iron that binds O₂; interactions between subunits allow cooperative binding, so oxygen is loaded efficiently in the lungs and unloaded in tissues. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a dipeptide and a polypeptide.
items.answer: A dipeptide consists of two amino acids joined by one peptide bond; a polypeptide is a long chain of many amino acids.
items.markingKey: A dipeptide consists of two amino acids joined by one peptide bond; a polypeptide is a long chain of many amino acids. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does a protein lose its function when denatured even though its amino acid sequence is unchanged?
options: Function depends on a specific 3D shape, which is lost.
Function depends only on primary structure.
items.answer: Function depends on a specific 3D shape, which is lost.
items.markingKey: A. Shape determines function.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of insulin relates to its function.
items.answer: Insulin is a small globular protein of two chains held by disulfide bonds; its specific shape binds to complementary insulin receptors; it is soluble so it can travel in blood plasma from the pancreas to target cells.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Insulin is a small globular protein of two chains held by disulfide bonds; its specific shape binds to complementary insulin receptors; it is soluble so it can travel in blood plasma from the pancreas to target cells. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between α-helices and β-pleated sheets.
items.answer: In an α-helix the polypeptide coils, with hydrogen bonds between groups four amino acids apart in the same strand; in a β-pleated sheet adjacent stretches of chain lie side by side, hydrogen bonded between strands.
items.markingKey: In an α-helix the polypeptide coils, with hydrogen bonds between groups four amino acids apart in the same strand; in a β-pleated sheet adjacent stretches of chain lie side by side, hydrogen bonded between strands. items.stem: Outline one way in which the dietary combination of rice and lentils in South Asian cooking (dal-bhat) shows essential amino acids.
items.answer: Rice is low in lysine and lentils are low in methionine; together they supply all essential amino acids. Combining plant proteins with different deficiencies supplies all the amino acids the body cannot make.
items.markingKey: Context (Rice is low in lysine and lentils are low in methionine; together they supply all essential amino acids.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Combining plant proteins with different deficiencies supplies all the amino acids the body cannot make. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to essential amino acids.

Casein proteins denature/precipitate when pH changes alter their charges.

items.stem:
Samples of a protease from cod (a cold-water fish) (enzyme X) and a homologous enzyme from the archaeon Pyrococcus furiosus (enzyme Y) were held at different temperatures for 10 minutes, cooled to 25 °C and their remaining activity measured as a percentage of the untreated activity.

Temperature / °C | Enzyme X activity remaining / % | Enzyme Y activity remaining / %
30 | 100 | 100
40 | 97 | 100
50 | 66 | 100
60 | 10 | 100
70 | 1 | 97
80 | 0 | 67
90 | 0 | 11

(a) State the activity of enzyme X remaining after treatment at 60 °C. [1]
(b) Estimate the temperature at which each enzyme has lost half of its activity. [2]
(c) Compare the effect of temperature on enzymes X and Y. [2]
(d) Explain why activity was measured at 25 °C after cooling, rather than at the treatment temperature. [1]
(e) Explain the loss of activity of enzyme X at high temperatures. [3]
(f) Suggest how the structure of enzyme Y differs to make it more heat stable. [1]
(g) Suggest one industrial use of enzyme Y and justify it. [2]
items.answer: (a) 10 % (b) X ≈ 53 °C; Y ≈ 83 °C (c) Both retain full activity at low temperatures and lose activity as temperature rises; Y tolerates much higher temperatures before losing activity. (d) It measures only the permanent (irreversible) loss of activity due to denaturation, not the temporary effect of temperature on reaction rate. (e) Heat breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds/hydrophobic interactions maintaining tertiary structure; active site changes shape; substrate no longer binds; denaturation. (f) More disulfide bonds, ionic bonds (salt bridges) and hydrophobic interactions; more compact core. (g) PCR or biological washing powders/industrial processes at high temperature – remains active and reactions are faster at high temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 10 % (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation (M1); X 53 °C and Y 83 °C, accept ±2 °C (A1). (c) [2] Similarity (A1); difference with data (A1). (d) [1] Separates denaturation from effect on rate (R1). (e) [3] Weak bonds broken (A1); shape/active site changed (A1); irreversible denaturation (A1). (f) [1] Any valid structural difference (A1). (g) [2] Use (A1) with justification (R1).
